blocks.text: Heller takes it to mean primordial creation by God, since it might well be possible that living beings originally developed out of the earthy matter.

But who created the primordial matter, the earth, out of which the further development was to take place? It cannot, however, be our intention to enter here into a metaphysical inquiry, since our [p. 346] task is rather to demonstrate the existence of that zoophytic creature, and for this there are many weighty witnesses. Diodorus Siculus (Bibliothek B. 1, ch. 10) says: The Egyptians maintain that the first human beings came into being in Egypt, by virtue of the good climate of the country and the fertility of the Nile. The first origin of animals among them they prove by the fact that even now in the Thebaid, at certain times, the land produces so many and such large mice that those who see it marvel at it. Some of them are formed as far as the breast and the forefeet and acquire motion, while the remaining part of the body is still a clod of earth*). Aelian (Thierg. 2, 56) says: As I hear, when hail and rain fall in the Thebaid, mice come into being which consist partly of muddy filth, partly of flesh**).
Aelian speaks further and in more detail about this zoophyte in book 6, ch. 41.

Jacobs, in the scholia on the first passage, also cites Basilios (the Saint, who lived in the 4th century of the Christian era and was thus a contemporary of the Talmudists), who says: Around Thebes and Egypt the ground fills with earth-mice as soon as it rains heavily in the hot days***); he further cites Pliny h. n. 9, 58, 84†), Plutarch part 2, p. 637 and Philopon. in Gen. ch. 1, p. 196; cf. also Ovid (Metam. 1, v. 422 ff.). With so many witnesses, the Talmud can surely not be reproached for speaking in definite terms of this zoophyte, and Leopold Löw (see Ha-Chalutz part 3, p. 168) would have done well to read the above sources before losing himself in irony about the Talmud.

(Appendix.) In Sanhedrin 91a it is said: A doubter of the resurrection of the dead was told to go into the field and see how the mouse, today half of flesh and half [p. 347] of earth, is already wholly flesh on the very next day.

Here Rashi says: “The mouse is called אשקירול”; but this foreign word can only be the French Ecureuil, which however means squirrel (§. 140), as it is also used in this sense by Gerson in the passage cited there. Rashi knew neither our zoophyte nor the nature of the dormouse, which is why this foreign word is also inapplicable to the latter animal (A. Sara 68b).
The statement that the mouse detaches itself from the earth and becomes wholly flesh I have found mentioned nowhere.

We treat the pearl mussel at this point, and the fan mussel in the following article, because both attach themselves by their byssus, either, like the former, to the bottom of the sea, or, like the latter, to stones, and thus in a certain sense belong to the zoophytes; we have not, however, treated them above among the shellfish or molluscs, because they are not mentioned as animals in the Talmud; it mentions only the pearl, and only in a mineralogical respect. The phrase אבנים טובות ומרגליות “precious stones and pearls” occurs frequently, from which it follows that the Talmud regards the pearl not as a stone consisting of earthy matter but, as is correct, as the hardening of an animal substance; which is why one need not, with Jellinek (Nachträge zu Sefer Chachamim p. 6), think of the Arabic and Persian دُرّ [durr] (pearl) in the Talmudic words אבן טובה יש בכרכי הים ודרה שמה (Megilla 12a); for apart from the fact that pearls were certainly not used for laying floors, the pearl is also not to be regarded as a stone. What is presumably correct is, as Rosenmüller (Bibl. Alterth. 4, 1, p. 23) has shown, that דר means a kind of alabaster with a mother-of-pearl lustre; cf. also Winer (R.-W. s.v. Marmor).

In Joma 75a it is said: The pearl is white, i.e. milk-white*); yet it is known that oriental pearls tend toward [p. 348] flesh colour, and also that those that have grown old, after some fifty years, appear yellowish. See Voigt l. c. 3, p. 503.

A Talmudist attests (Sanhedrin 100a) that up to his time no pearl had been found the size of the egg of a species of turtledove ציצילהא (§. 252); Voigt (ibid. 3, p. 504), however, relates that someone in Moscow saw a pearl that was one inch in diameter and was valued at one and a half million paper roubles.
A fine proverb occurs in the Jerusalem Talmud (Berachot C, 9, fol. 12, d): מרגלית דליה לה טימי כל שמשבח בה פגמה “he who praises the priceless pearl disparages it.”
The name מרגלית corresponds to the Latin margarita, with interchange of the ל and the R-sound, f. §. 467.
A string of pearls (פוריל"ש) is called חומרי פחכייתא (Kiduschin 9a), the pearl-borer: נוקב מרגליות (Choschen Mispat §. 420, 15).

In the Talmud the proverb often occurs: אי לאו דלינא חספא לא משתכחת מרגניתא תוהיה “Had I not brought up the stone (so Buxdorf Lex. p. 1250), you would not have found the pearl beneath it” (Jebamoth 92b and frequently). The Tosephot (B. mez. 17b, s.v. אי) come close to natural-historical accuracy; they say: “There are on the sea bottom broad stones, looking like potsherds, beneath which pearls are found.” They refer to B. Kama 91a, where it is said proverbially of one who labours in vain over something: “You descend into the depths of the sea but bring up only a potsherd”; i.e., he brings up the shell that is without a pearl. For in many mussels, which open only ten days after being caught, one finds nothing, but on the other hand many pearls in a single one.
מרגניתא may perhaps specifically denote the fan-mussel pearl, as distinct from מרגליות, the pearl mussel.
